chapters.title: Chapter 5: Matching the Method to the Business

lessons.title: Valuing Banks and NBFCs: Why FCF-Based DCF Breaks and What Works Instead

children.text: Every method in this course so far has rested on free cash flow: cash the business generates after paying for what it needs to keep running. Apply that idea to a bank and it falls apart immediately. A bank's "raw material" is money. It takes deposits and borrowings, lends them out, and earns the spread. Its debt is not financing the business, it is the business. That single fact breaks enterprise value, breaks EV/EBITDA and breaks the FCFF model. Banks and NBFCs make up a large share of the Nifty 50, so any serious Indian investor needs a different toolkit.

body.text: For a lender, debt is inventory, not financing. Skip enterprise value entirely and value the equity directly, using residual income, dividends or a P/B anchored to return on equity. The binding constraint on growth is regulatory capital, not cash.

children.text: Why the Standard Toolkit Breaks

body.caption: What goes wrong when you apply FCFF and EV multiples to a lender
headers: Why it fails for a bank or NBFC

cells: Enterprise value = market cap + debt - cash
Deposits and borrowings are operating inputs, not financing. Adding them produces a meaningless number that rises as the bank grows.
Interest expense is a cost of goods sold for a lender, so profit before interest is not a real measure of anything.
FCFF = EBIT(1 - t) + D&A - capex - ΔNWC
Capex and working capital barely matter. Growth consumes regulatory capital instead, which the formula ignores.
Two identical banks with different deposit bases would show wildly different multiples.
Cash on the balance sheet as a surplus asset
Cash and balances with the RBI are working inventory, partly required by law, not distributable surplus.

body.text: This is also why you must never lump a lending subsidiary into a consolidated EV/EBITDA multiple for a group, whether it is an auto company with a captive finance arm or a conglomerate with an NBFC. Value the lender separately on P/B or residual income, and add it to the parts, as the sum-of-the-parts lesson later in this chapter shows.

children.text: What Constrains a Lender: Capital, Not Cash
A lender cannot simply grow its loan book as fast as demand allows. Every rupee lent must be backed by regulatory capital, measured by the
capital adequacy ratio
. That makes profitability, growth and capital a single linked system.

markDefs.definition: Regulatory capital as a percentage of risk-weighted assets. In India it is called CRAR (capital to risk-weighted assets ratio) for banks, with minimum levels set by the RBI under the Basel III framework.

body.caption: A lender can grow its book at this rate without raising fresh equity

children.text: Narmadapuram Private Bank, the fictional lender from Chapter 4, earns an ROE of 18.0% and wants to grow its loan book at 15.0% a year. It must therefore retain 83.3% of its profit, paying out only 16.7% as dividends. Grow faster than ROE allows and the bank must raise fresh equity, diluting existing shareholders. This is why fast-growing Indian banks and NBFCs return to the market with qualified institutional placements and rights issues, and why per-share value, not total value, is what matters.

body.caption: Indicative minimum capital requirements in India

cells: Minimum CRAR of 9%, plus a capital conservation buffer of 2.5%
Higher than the Basel III global minimum; systemically important banks carry an additional surcharge
Minimum CRAR of 15%, with Tier 1 of at least 10%
Reflects their reliance on wholesale funding
Additional requirements under the RBI's supervisory framework
Weak banks can be placed under Prompt Corrective Action, restricting growth and dividends

body.text: Capital ratios are a valuation input, not a compliance footnote. A bank sitting close to its minimum has three choices: slow down, raise equity and dilute, or take more risk. All three affect per-share value. A bank with surplus capital can grow for years without returning to shareholders.

children.text: Method 1: Residual Income
The cleanest model for a lender is the
residual income model
, because it uses the two things a bank reports reliably: book value and return on equity.

markDefs.definition: A valuation model that starts from book value and adds the present value of profits earned above the cost of equity in each future year. Equity value = book value + present value of (ROE - Ke) × opening book.

body.latex: \text{Equity value} = B_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{(\text{ROE}_t - K_e) \times B_{t-1}}{(1 + K_e)^t} + \text{Terminal value}
body.caption: Book value today, plus the present value of every rupee earned above the cost of equity

children.text: The logic matches Chapter 4's P/B rule exactly. A bank earning its cost of equity adds nothing to book value. In steady state, with an ROE of 16.0%, a cost of equity of 13.0% and growth of 7.0%, both methods give the same answer on a ₹20,000 crore book: justified P/B of 1.50× gives ₹30,000 crore, and residual income gives ₹30,000 crore.
A two-stage worked example

Now model Narmadapuram properly. It has a book value of ₹20,000 crore and 500 crore shares, so ₹40.0 per share. Assume it earns 18.0% ROE and grows its book 15.0% a year for 5 years, after which competition and scale bring ROE down to 14.0% and growth to 7.0% forever. Its cost of equity is 13.0%.

body.caption: Narmadapuram Private Bank: residual income build-up (₹ crore, illustrative)

stats.label: PV of residual income, years 1 to 5
stats.context: Earning 18.0% against a 13.0% cost of equity

children.text: The model values Narmadapuram at ₹28,223 crore, or ₹56.4 per share, which is 1.41 times its current book value. Notice where the value comes from: ₹20,000 crore is simply the capital already in the business, and only ₹8,223 crore is created by earning above the cost of equity. If ROE fell to 13.0%, the bank would be worth its book value and nothing more.

body.text: Residual income has a practical advantage over dividend discount models for Indian lenders: most of the value sits in book value, a reported number, rather than in distant forecast dividends. That makes the model less sensitive to terminal assumptions than a DCF on a manufacturing company, where the terminal value often carries 70% or more of the total.

children.text: Method 2: Decomposing ROE with the ROA Tree
Since ROE drives everything, do not treat it as a single assumption. Break it into the drivers a bank actually manages, each measured as a percentage of average assets.

body.caption: Return on assets multiplied by leverage. A lender earns a thin margin on a large balance sheet.
Narmadapuram Private Bank: ROA tree (% of average assets, illustrative)

cells: Interest earned minus interest paid, the core spread
Processing fees, third-party distribution, forex, cards
The buffer available to absorb loan losses
Provisions for bad loans, as a share of assets
Around 1.3% to 1.8% is typical for a well-run Indian bank

children.text: Now stress one line. If credit cost doubles from 0.8% to 1.6% of assets, a change that sounds small, ROA falls to 0.8% and ROE to 8.3%. At a 13.0% cost of equity, the justified P/B collapses from around 1.31× to 0.21×. This is the single most important sensitivity in bank valuation, and it is why asset quality dominates every discussion of Indian lenders.

body.title: One line item, two valuations: the effect of doubling credit cost

children.text: Asset Quality: The Numbers That Decide Everything

body.caption: What to check before valuing any Indian lender

cells: Bad loans as a share of advances, before and after provisions
How much of bad loans is already provided for. Low PCR means future profits are at risk.
Fresh loans turning bad during the period, the leading indicator
Provisions as a percentage of average advances
Loans given relief that may still turn bad
Unsecured retail, microfinance and SME lending carry higher credit costs than housing or gold loans

children.text: When bad loans are large or under-provided, adjust book value before applying any multiple, as Chapter 4 showed with price to adjusted book value. Note also that banks and NBFCs follow different provisioning frameworks: banks apply the RBI's income recognition and asset classification norms, while NBFCs report under Ind AS with expected credit loss provisioning, so headline provision numbers are not directly comparable.
NBFCs: The Same Model, Sharper Risks

columns.label: Banks
points: Funding: low-cost deposits, especially current and savings accounts
Higher regulation: CRR, SLR, priority sector lending
Valuation anchor: P/B against ROE, residual income

columns.label: NBFCs
points: Funding: bank borrowings, NCDs, commercial paper, securitisation
No deposit franchise for most; funding can dry up quickly
Lighter regulation, but tightened in recent years under a scale-based framework
Minimum CRAR of 15% for large non-deposit-taking NBFCs
Valuation anchor: P/B against ROE, with a sharper focus on funding and liquidity

body.text: Asset-liability mismatch is the risk that ends NBFCs. Borrowing short-term money to fund long-term loans works until lenders stop rolling over the funding. After a large infrastructure financier defaulted in 2018, funding costs across the Indian NBFC sector rose sharply and several lenders were forced to shrink. No P/B multiple protects you from a funding freeze: check the maturity profile of borrowings against the maturity of the loan book.

cells: A rising cost of funds squeezes margins quickly if loans are fixed rate
Reliance on short-term commercial paper is fragile; a diversified, longer-tenure mix is safer
Disclosed in the notes; look for large negative gaps in short buckets
Upfront gains can flatter profits; check how much of earnings is recurring
Change both risk sharing and reported book size
Loans to group companies are a governance red flag

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Justified P/B for a lender
body.prompt: An NBFC has a sustainable ROE of 15%, a cost of equity of 13.5% and long-term growth of 6%. What is its justified P/B? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Justified P/B = (15% - 6%) ÷ (13.5% - 6%) = 9 ÷ 7.5 = 1.20×. Only the gap between ROE and the cost of equity creates value above book.

body.title: First-year residual income
body.prompt: A bank has a book value of ₹8,000 crore, an ROE of 17% and a cost of equity of 12.5%. What is its residual income in year 1, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Residual income = (ROE - Ke) × opening book = (17% - 12.5%) × ₹8,000 crore = ₹360 crore. This is the profit earned above what shareholders require, and the present value of all such amounts is what the bank is worth above its book value.

body.title: Why not EV/EBITDA?
body.question: Why is EV/EBITDA inappropriate for valuing a bank?
options: Because banks do not report EBITDA to the RBI
Because deposits and borrowings are the bank's raw material rather than financing, so enterprise value is meaningless, and interest expense is a core cost rather than a financing item
Because EBITDA is always negative for banks
body.explanation: Enterprise value assumes debt funds the business. For a lender, deposits and borrowings are inputs it lends out, so adding them to market cap produces a number that grows with the balance sheet and means nothing. Interest expense is a cost of goods sold, so profit before interest is not meaningful either.

body.title: The ROE identity
body.textWithBlank: For a lender, ROE equals return on assets multiplied by ___.
body.explanation: ROE = ROA × (assets ÷ equity). Lenders earn a thin return on a large balance sheet, and capital adequacy rules cap how much leverage they can use.

body.title: The fast-growing NBFC at 5 times book
body.scenario: Priyanka, an investor in Pune, is looking at a listed NBFC lending to small businesses. It trades at 5 times book value. Its ROE is 19%, its cost of equity is about 14%, and its loan book has grown 40% a year for three years. Reading the disclosures, she finds: gross NPAs of 2.1% with a provision coverage ratio of 42%; 55% of borrowings maturing within one year against an average loan tenure of four years; capital adequacy of 16.5%, just above the minimum; and a large part of recent profit coming from upfront gains on assigning loans to banks.
body.prompt: What does the 5 times book multiple imply, and what are the risks Priyanka should weigh?
body.modelAnswer:
1. What 5× book implies. With an ROE of 19% and a 14% cost of equity, even permanent growth at 10% would justify roughly (19 - 10) ÷ (14 - 10) = 2.25 times book. A multiple of 5 times assumes ROE stays high while the book compounds for a very long time, which is a demanding expectation for an unsecured or small-business lender.
2. Growth needs capital. Growing 40% a year with a 19% ROE is impossible from retained earnings alone. The NBFC must keep raising equity, so existing shareholders face dilution. With capital adequacy at 16.5%, just above the 15% minimum, a raise is likely soon.
3. Asset quality may be understated. A provision coverage ratio of 42% is low, so future provisions will hit profits if slippages rise. She should adjust book value for under-provisioning before applying any multiple.
4. Asset-liability mismatch. Funding 55% short-term against four-year loans is exactly the structure that caused severe stress in the Indian NBFC sector after 2018. If funding markets tighten, the company must shrink, refinance at higher cost or sell assets.
5. Earnings quality. Upfront assignment gains are not recurring. She should estimate ROE excluding them, since valuation depends on sustainable ROE.

Conclusion: the multiple prices in sustained high growth and high returns with no accidents. She should build a residual income model with a lower sustainable ROE, explicit dilution from future equity raises, and a stress case with higher credit costs, then compare the result with the market price.

cards.definition: Net interest income as a percentage of average earning assets. The core spread a lender earns.
Provisions for bad loans as a percentage of average advances or assets.
The share of gross bad loans already provided for. Low coverage means future profits are at risk.
Capital to risk-weighted assets ratio. The regulatory capital a lender must hold against its loans.
(ROE - cost of equity) × opening book value. Profit earned above what shareholders require.
Funding long-tenure loans with short-tenure borrowings, creating refinancing risk.
The forward-looking provisioning approach used by NBFCs under Ind AS, unlike the RBI norms banks follow.

points: For lenders, debt is raw material. Enterprise value, EV/EBITDA and FCFF do not apply.
Value the equity directly using residual income, dividend discount models or P/B anchored to ROE.
Residual income = book value + present value of (ROE - cost of equity) × opening book. A lender earning its cost of equity is worth book value.
Growth is limited by capital: sustainable growth equals ROE × retention. Faster growth means equity raises and dilution.
Break ROE into the ROA tree. Credit cost is the most powerful single variable, and small changes swing the justified P/B sharply.
For NBFCs, add funding mix and asset-liability maturity checks. A funding freeze, not a valuation multiple, is the real risk.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Narmadapuram Private Bank, the NBFC described and the individuals named are fictional, and all figures are illustrative. Regulatory capital requirements are summarised and change over time; refer to current RBI circulars. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
